title: Token-slice priority scheduling and starvation guardrails for prefill/decode
creator: Alex Kim
description: Problem: Our current prefill/decode scheduler favors single large requests (long prefill or long decodes) which increases tail latency for small interactive requests and creates occasional customer unfairness under moderate contention. Goal: Implement a token-slice priority policy that splits large requests across scheduler phases and enforces starvation guardrails so low-latency requests meet p50/p95 targets for interactive customers without dramatically sacrificing overall throughput. Scope: runtime scheduler and admission controller changes; light-weight metrics; no model architecture changes. Out of scope: full multi-tenant accounting refunds, billing changes, or kernel-level attention changes (those are separate tickets).
acceptance_criteria: Scheduler implements token-slice-based priority where long prefill requests are split into configurable slices and interleaved with decode work according to priority weights
Starvation guardrail prevents any request from being postponed > 200ms under 95th percentile GPU utilization for standard-tier customers
End-to-end e2e perf tests show interactive 0.5s p95 improvement for small requests under mixed workload (1M tokens/min baseline) with <8% throughput regression on synthetic long-stream workload
Feature toggled behind runtime feature flag with a canary rollout and telemetry available in console (per-route latency breakdown)
decision: Adopt token-slice priority with dynamic weight adjustment. Default policy: slice large prefill into 256-token units, schedule round-robin across active requests with priority boost for interactive SLA-tagged tokens. Dynamic weight adjustment controller scales slices per-customer up to a configured max to keep p95 targets. This balances latency vs throughput while keeping implementation surface minimal.
tradeoffs: Pros: predictable latency for interactive requests, simpler to reason about fairness, incremental rollout

Cons: added scheduler complexity, potential minor throughput loss due to more context switches between prefill/decode, requires careful kernel selection to avoid repeated kernel warmups for short slices
Mitigations: co-locate slices on same GPU to reuse kernels and KV caches; use a slice-size heuristic tuned per-model family
perf_summary: Initial bench (A100, 16k context) with mixed workload (70% short interactive 16-token queries, 30% long prefill 8k tokens): token-slice policy (256-token slices) improved short-query p95 from 420ms -> 180ms, p99 from 920ms -> 430ms. Aggregate throughput dropped 6% vs baseline. Kernel-level observations: small slices increased kernel launch count by ~12%, but KV cache reuse across slices avoided memory thrashing when slices pinned to same worker.
